subtitle: Learn to make stretch assignments and other development opportunities visible, usable and tied to relevant evidence. Throughout, fair employment procedures remain in place.
scope: For DHS supervisors and leaders assigning developmental work or supporting career growth. These learning activities do not authorize promotions, compensation changes, work-out-of-class arrangements or exceptions to recruitment, bargaining and classification rules. Confirm applicable requirements with HR before acting. Use invented employee details in course practice.
introTranscript: A stretch assignment gives someone a supported opportunity to develop a capability through real work. It should not be a hidden audition, an unpaid promise of promotion or a favor limited to familiar colleagues. Fair access requires more than a broad announcement: the purpose, criteria, interest route, workload and feedback need to be usable. Across six lessons you will separate learning work from formal employment decisions, explain an opportunity before selection, compare relevant evidence, provide support, recognize contribution and review the process. Different employees may choose different opportunities. The aim is an explainable process that builds capability, not identical career outcomes or a ranking of people.

lessons.title: Separate development from a formal employment decision
lessons.summary: Clarify what the assignment is and which authority or procedure applies before inviting participation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a developmental task from a proposed change in role or employment terms.
objectives: Distinguish a developmental task from a proposed change in role or employment terms.
Write the capability and work result a stretch assignment is intended to develop.
Identify a question that requires HR or another responsible authority before implementation.
takeaways: A stretch assignment has a learning and work purpose.
Formal employment changes need their applicable process.
Do not promise promotion as an informal reward.
lessons.statement: Explain the opportunity honestly before anyone invests time in it.

image.caption: A clear purpose distinguishes developmental work from an employment promise.

intro.heading: Name the kind of opportunity
intro.body:
A leader may call any additional responsibility a stretch assignment. The label does not determine the actual employment requirements. A short, supported task within a role is different from sustained duties that may affect classification, compensation or work-out-of-class arrangements. A formal promotion is different again. Confirm the applicable process with HR or the responsible role rather than using a learning label to avoid a required procedure.

Begin with a purpose sentence. What capability can the employee develop, and what useful result will the work produce? An analyst might practice facilitating a small review meeting while preparing a decision summary. The assignment should have boundaries, support and feedback. “Prove that you deserve advancement” is not a clear capability or an honest description of the employment process.

State what the assignment does not guarantee. Relevant experience may help an employee develop evidence for future opportunities, but it should not be presented as an automatic promotion, pay change or appointment. Minnesota’s recruitment and selection policy applies to covered selections; particular arrangements may also involve bargaining agreements or compensation plans. This course does not determine those requirements for a specific position.

Check whether the task can be undertaken with the employee’s current authority and access. Learning is not a reason to make a restricted service decision or use records outside approved access. Clarify which decisions remain with the supervisor and when the employee should request review. A real task can be meaningful without transferring every responsibility at once.

Finally, explain the time commitment and how existing work will be managed. A development promise is not usable if it simply adds unbounded work. Before inviting interest, resolve the basic purpose and authority questions so that people can make an informed choice rather than discover the terms after selection.

lessons.keyStatement: Calling work developmental does not change the formal rules that apply to the arrangement.

flashcards.back: A bounded work opportunity designed to develop a capability with appropriate support and feedback.
A formal employment decision governed by the applicable recruitment and appointment procedures.
Relevant examples that demonstrate a skill or knowledge needed for work.
The limit on what a role may decide, access or promise.
The agreed way the new task fits with existing duties and authorized time.

items.title: A short supported task
items.body: A limited task can develop a capability when its result, review point and support are clear. Confirm that it fits the role and current authority. Do not assume every small assignment is exempt from relevant procedures; ask the responsible role when the arrangement or duties raise a question.

items.title: An extended higher-level responsibility
items.body: The duration and duties may raise classification, compensation or bargaining questions. Seek HR guidance before treating the arrangement as informal learning. A development goal does not justify asking someone to perform a different role indefinitely on an unsupported promise of future recognition.

items.title: A promised future appointment
items.body: A leader’s enthusiasm is not an appointment process. Explain how the experience may build relevant evidence while preserving applicable selection requirements. Do not tell an employee that completing an assignment guarantees promotion or that other applicants will not be considered.

tabs.label: Capability
tabs.body: A capability is the skill the assignment is intended to develop, such as comparing alternatives and explaining uncertainty. A vague promise to build leadership presence makes the learning difficult to examine. Name the actual work through which the employee can demonstrate progress. This creates a useful learning purpose without converting a personality impression into a selection criterion.

tabs.label: Result
tabs.body: A result describes the bounded product or decision support and who needs it. Producing a short analysis differs from taking over every task in a larger role indefinitely. Clarifying the boundary allows support and time to be planned. If the duties grow, revisit the agreement rather than treating the initial acceptance as consent to unlimited additional work.

tabs.label: Authority
tabs.body: Authority determines whether the proposed duties, compensation, classification, access and bargaining requirements permit the arrangement. A learning label does not settle those questions. Confirm them with HR and responsible roles before inviting participation. A supervisor can encourage development without promising a promotion or authorizing work outside the employee’s approved responsibilities.

check.question: A supervisor wants an employee to perform higher-level duties for many months and calls it a stretch assignment. What should happen first?
check.correct: Confirm applicable HR, compensation, classification and bargaining requirements before making the arrangement or promising a future result.
wrong: Use the learning label to avoid reviewing the duties.
Promise a promotion if the employee accepts without questions.
Ask the employee to work outside approved access so they gain experience.
check.feedbackCorrect: The arrangement must be examined on its actual duties and requirements, not merely its informal label.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling higher-level duties learning does not remove compensation, classification or bargaining questions. Promising promotion in return for unquestioning acceptance bypasses future authority and can pressure the employee. Working outside approved access creates another procedural problem. Review the actual duties and applicable requirements before arranging the work.

items.text: Practice facilitating a bounded review with an experienced colleague.
Determine whether extended duties require a formal work arrangement.
Completion guarantees an appointment without selection.
Produce a short decision summary and receive feedback on evidence use.
Confirm classification and bargaining requirements with HR.
Accept extra work now and receive an unapproved pay change later.

lessons.next: Next, make the invitation visible and understandable.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Omar asks Leila to lead a higher-level function for an extended period. He calls it development and says she will be promoted afterward. Neither the duties nor the promise have been reviewed with HR.
options: Clarify the duties and learning purpose, consult responsible HR authority and remove any unsupported promotion promise.
Rename the work as volunteering so no procedure applies.
responses: Enthusiasm does not resolve formal requirements or make the promise authorized.
This makes the arrangement honest and preserves the processes that apply to actual duties and selection.
Renaming work does not change its employment implications.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice assignment purpose with capability, result, duration boundary, support and authority questions. Mark every outcome you cannot promise.

move.control: You can clarify the learning purpose and obtain responsible guidance before inviting participation.
move.failure: An informal opportunity becomes a hidden employment arrangement supported only by a promise.
move.next: Review the type and authority of the next proposed stretch assignment before discussing participation.

lessons.title: Make the opportunity visible before choosing someone
lessons.summary: Explain purpose, criteria and a usable route to express interest without assuming who will want the work.
lessons.objective: Write an invitation that names the purpose, requirements and interest route.
objectives: Write an invitation that names the purpose, requirements and interest route.
Identify an informal practice that gives familiar employees an early advantage.
Distinguish asking about interest from making an identity-based assumption.
takeaways: Ask about interest rather than assuming it.
lessons.statement: People cannot express informed interest in an opportunity they cannot find or understand.

image.caption: A useful invitation explains the work before interest is assessed.

intro.heading: Give people an informed chance to consider the work
intro.body:
Some opportunities begin through casual conversation. A supervisor mentions an interesting project to a colleague they see often, and the colleague begins preparing before others hear about it. The later announcement may appear open while the decision already feels settled. Where the applicable process permits a broader invitation, make the purpose and route visible before the choice rather than using an announcement to confirm an informal preference.

A useful invitation explains the capability, work result, relevant entry requirements, time commitment, support and selection route. It should say how to ask a question and express interest. Avoid unexplained shorthand and a vague request for “high-potential people.” Employees need enough information to decide whether the opportunity fits their goals and available arrangements.

Do not assume interest from age, family responsibilities, disability, background or communication style. A person may want an opportunity that the supervisor would not have predicted. Another may decline for reasons they do not need to disclose in a learning exercise. Ask through the appropriate process and explain the commitment rather than deciding on the employee’s behalf.

Check whether the route is usable. A very short response window, a meeting-only announcement or a form that asks for unnecessary personal detail may restrict practical access. Follow actual posting and selection rules where they apply; this course does not invent a universal announcement period. If an urgent task permits a different arrangement, document the responsible decision and avoid describing it as an open process when it was not.

An invitation does not guarantee selection or equal outcomes. It creates a clearer opportunity to understand the work and provide relevant evidence. When someone is not selected, the criteria and available next steps should remain explainable. The leader should be able to describe the process without relying on “everyone knows who is ready.”

inThisLesson: Publish criteria through the appropriate route.
Check practical access to the invitation.
lessons.keyStatement: An open process begins before a favored person has already been chosen.

items.title: A familiar colleague hears first
items.body: Early information can affect preparation and perceived fairness. Check the applicable process and make the invitation usable before selection where appropriate. Do not pretend that an already settled choice is open. If a responsible urgent assignment is made directly, explain the arrangement accurately rather than staging a symbolic competition.

items.title: The invitation asks for high potential
items.body: The phrase can conceal an unspoken preference for confidence or similarity. Name the capability and relevant evidence instead. Explain what can be developed through the assignment and what is required at entry. This makes the opportunity understandable without lowering actual work requirements.

items.title: A supervisor predicts who will decline
items.body: Predictions about private circumstances should not replace an informed choice. Offer the relevant information and route for questions. Do not require disclosure of family, medical or cultural details to justify interest or decline. Formal support requests retain their responsible agency processes.

tabs.label: Purpose
tabs.body: Purpose explains the actual work and what can be learned from it. Employees can make an informed choice when the invitation describes a concrete analysis task rather than an unexplained prestige opportunity. Be honest about what it does not promise. Useful development evidence may support later consideration, but it does not guarantee an appointment.

tabs.label: Practical terms
tabs.body: Practical terms describe time, workload and support. An invitation can appear open while relying on evening effort or an unavailable colleague. Confirm approved arrangements and disclose unresolved conditions so employees do not have to guess the costs of accepting. Workable support helps distinguish a real opportunity from a task that merely shifts extra burdens onto willing people.

tabs.label: Interest route
tabs.body: An interest route explains how to learn more or express interest through the applicable process. Employees outside the supervisor’s familiar network should be able to find and use it. Do not assume someone will decline because of caregiving or another private circumstance. Provide relevant information and allow choice, while keeping criteria and authority intact.

check.question: A leader assumes an employee with caregiving responsibilities would not want an assignment. What is the better approach?
check.correct: Provide relevant opportunity information through the appropriate process and let the employee express interest without requiring private justification.
wrong: Exclude the employee to protect them from a demanding task.
Ask for family details before allowing an expression of interest.
Select the employee automatically to correct the assumption.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves informed choice and relevant criteria without making a private circumstance the decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Protective exclusion still substitutes the supervisor’s assumption for the employee’s informed choice. Demanding family details adds unnecessary private information. Automatic selection skips relevant criteria rather than repairing access. Provide the real terms and appropriate interest route, allowing the employee to decide whether to participate without private justification.

items.text: The invitation names the result, criteria, time and question contact.
A favored person prepares weeks before anyone else hears.
The leader excludes a colleague based on guessed family responsibilities.
Employees receive a clear route to express interest under the applicable process.
The open announcement is sent after the choice is settled.
Quiet communication is interpreted as no career interest.

lessons.next: Next, compare relevant evidence without changing the criteria.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Marta wants a colleague to lead a small process review. She tells her usual lunch companion first, then says that Kofi is probably too busy with family to be interested. The review can use an appropriate wider interest invitation.
options: Make purpose, criteria and support visible through the appropriate route, and let employees describe their own interest.
Keep the informal approach because Marta knows the team well.
Ask Kofi to prove he has no family commitments.
responses: This gives employees a usable choice and reduces the advantage of informal familiarity.
Familiarity can conceal untested assumptions and unequal information.
Private proof is not a relevant interest criterion and creates an unnecessary burden.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice invitation with purpose, capability, criteria, commitment, support, question contact and interest route. Ask a colleague to identify what remains unclear.

move.control: You can make information understandable and ask about interest through responsible procedures.
move.failure: The announcement appears open but functions as confirmation of a familiar person’s earlier selection.
move.next: Review who can discover the next opportunity before choosing participants.

lessons.title: Compare capability evidence with stable criteria
lessons.summary: Use criteria relevant to the work and examine assumptions that substitute visibility or similarity for readiness.
lessons.objective: Connect a selection criterion to a capability needed for the assignment.
objectives: Connect a selection criterion to a capability needed for the assignment.
Compare two practice examples against the same criterion.
Identify a change in criteria that favors a preferred employee.
takeaways: Visibility is not the same as capability.
lessons.statement: Explain the choice through relevant evidence rather than who feels most familiar.

image.caption: Stable criteria make the basis of a choice easier to examine.

intro.heading: Assess readiness for this opportunity
intro.body:
Choosing a participant requires judgment, but the judgment should have an explainable basis. A leader may prefer someone who speaks first in meetings or whose work history resembles their own. Those features can create confidence without demonstrating the capability the assignment requires. Begin with criteria tied to the work and the support available, then examine relevant evidence consistently.

Distinguish what must be present at entry from what the assignment is intended to develop. If facilitation is the learning goal, requiring extensive facilitation experience may defeat the purpose unless the actual task needs it. If a particular technical skill is essential for safe or accurate work, do not ignore it. Confirm applicable selection requirements with the responsible role rather than rewriting them informally.

Invite evidence relevant to the same question. An employee could describe a time they organized conflicting information, handled a bounded decision or incorporated feedback. Assess the capability demonstrated, not the prestige of the setting or confidence of the telling. Do not infer absence of skill merely because an employee has had fewer visible assignments; that may itself be an opportunity-access question.

Keep criteria stable through the decision. If a leader changes the weighting after seeing a favored employee’s example, the process becomes difficult to defend. A genuine problem with the criteria should be handled through the appropriate process, with a clear explanation, rather than a private adjustment for one person. Formal promotions and covered selections retain their approved assessment rules.

Record the relevant reasoning in the appropriate channel and give a useful explanation. The employee does not need a secret “potential” label. A practical response can describe the capability evidence, the selection basis and another appropriate development route. This is different from guaranteeing the next opportunity or disclosing another employee’s private information.

inThisLesson: Separate entry needs from learning goals.
Explain the choice and next steps.
lessons.keyStatement: A defensible choice uses criteria established for the work before a preferred person appears.

items.title: Confidence is treated as readiness
items.body: Confidence may affect presentation but is not proof of the underlying capability. Ask what the work requires and which example demonstrates it. A clear written explanation or thoughtful preparation may provide relevant evidence even when a person is less visibly assertive. Do not erase actual communication requirements; make them specific.

items.title: Previous visibility becomes the main criterion
items.body: An employee who has already received public assignments may have more recognizable examples. Examine whether the new opportunity really requires that prior visibility or whether other evidence can demonstrate capability. The aim is not to disregard experience, but to avoid making previous access an unexplained prerequisite.

items.title: The weighting changes after review
items.body: A criterion adjustment designed to favor a person undermines consistency. If the criteria are genuinely unsuitable, seek the appropriate process for revising or restarting the decision. Keep the reasoning visible and prospective rather than moving the goalposts privately.

tabs.label: Same question
tabs.body: The same capability question should require comparable relevant evidence through the applicable process. Accepting familiarity for one employee but demanding extensive proof from another changes the standard. Explain what is being examined and how information may be supplied. Consistency concerns a usable evidence opportunity, not simply repeating identical words while access or support differs.

tabs.label: Work connection
tabs.body: The work connection explains what an example demonstrates for this assignment. An impressive title or public presentation may attract attention without establishing the analytical skill needed. Examine the person’s actual contribution and reasoning. A quieter example may be relevant, while a prestigious context can still leave the key capability uncertain.

tabs.label: Reasoned choice
tabs.body: A reasoned choice connects evidence, agreed criteria and available support. Moving the standard after seeing a favored person’s example undermines that explanation. Preserve the original basis and obtain responsible advice if a requirement needs review. Keep actual personnel information in approved channels; a course exercise is not a separate system for ranking employees.

check.question: A supervisor raises the importance of presentation style after reading a favored employee’s example. What is the concern?
check.correct: The criteria may be moving to favor a person rather than remaining connected to the work and established evidence approach.
wrong: Any supervisor preference automatically overrides the announced criteria.
The favored employee must be diagnosed as biased.
The correct response is to disregard all relevant experience.
check.feedbackCorrect: The concern is the decision process and its consistency, not a diagnosis of a person.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A supervisor’s preference does not automatically replace agreed criteria. Diagnosing the favored employee as biased misdirects a process concern toward a person without evidence. Discarding all relevant experience also loses the basis for comparison. Examine whether the standard moved, preserve the evidence and seek responsible review where needed.

items.text: An example shows how the employee organized conflicting information accurately.
The employee seems like the supervisor’s younger self.
A new weighting appears only after a preferred example is reviewed.
A work sample demonstrates the required analysis skill.
The employee is selected mainly for always speaking first.
The published criterion is removed to fit a familiar employee.

lessons.next: Next, make the selected opportunity workable through support and workload.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Two employees express interest in a process review. Inez gives a careful example of organizing evidence; Theo is more familiar to supervisor Jules and has a confident speaking style. The stated criteria emphasize evidence organization and reliable follow-through.
options: Choose Theo because confidence feels like leadership.
Change the criteria to make familiarity the deciding factor.
Compare the relevant examples against the established criteria and explain the supported choice.
responses: Confidence alone does not demonstrate the stated capabilities.
Changing the criteria for a preferred person compromises the process.
This keeps the decision tied to the work rather than an unexplained proxy.

lessons.transfer: Compare two invented examples against one capability criterion. Write the evidence and limitation for each without using personality or identity labels.

move.control: You can clarify criteria, examine relevant examples and seek guidance when formal selection rules apply.
move.failure: The selection is explained as potential while the actual basis is familiarity or changed criteria.
move.next: Before the next assignment choice, write the work connection for every criterion.

lessons.title: Make stretch work supported rather than unbounded
lessons.summary: Agree on workload, review points and authority so learning does not depend on hidden extra labor.
lessons.objective: Create a bounded assignment agreement with time, support and review points.
objectives: Create a bounded assignment agreement with time, support and review points.
Identify a workload cost that an invitation alone does not resolve.
Distinguish helpful support from taking over the employee’s work.
takeaways: Support is part of the opportunity.
lessons.statement: A development opportunity should make growth possible without hiding its costs.

image.caption: A supported assignment has clear limits and useful feedback.

intro.heading: Design the conditions for the work
intro.body:
After selection, a leader may assume the employee will manage the assignment alongside all existing duties. A stretch task can then require evening work, unclear authority or repeated dependence on a busy colleague. The employee receives the title of an opportunity while bearing its hidden costs. A workable agreement explains how the task fits with the job and which support makes learning possible.

Define the result and boundary. Which question or product is included, and which decisions remain elsewhere? Explain the relevant access and approval requirements. A project lead can coordinate a review without authority to change a service rule or direct every colleague’s work. Clear boundaries help the employee exercise judgment rather than avoid decisions altogether.

Discuss workload through the responsible process. Identify which duties continue, which may be adjusted and what authorized time or support is available. Do not promise overtime, compensation or flexibility outside your authority. If the workload cannot be made workable, reconsider the assignment rather than treating reluctance as low ambition. Employees should not need to disclose private circumstances to point out an unrealistic work plan.

Provide review points suited to the task. A brief early check may prevent a misunderstanding; later feedback can help refine judgment. Too little support leaves the employee guessing, while taking over the product prevents them from developing the capability. Ask the employee to explain options and reasoning, then give specific feedback connected to the work.

Revisit the agreement when conditions change. If the task expands, a deadline shifts or the colleague giving feedback becomes unavailable, update the plan and seek any required authority. Development should not mean accepting unlimited scope. The strongest experience combines contribution, supported practice and an honest account of the resources needed to do the work.

lessons.keyStatement: The assignment includes support and a manageable boundary, not just a request to do more.

items.title: The task expands silently
items.body: A small review can grow into a division-wide project. Pause to restate the result, authority, time and support. Confirm responsible approval for material changes. Do not assume the original agreement covers every additional responsibility or interpret a request for clarity as resistance to growth.

items.title: The colleague takes over
items.body: A colleague may rewrite the entire product to save time. Ask which parts the employee can revise with specific feedback and appropriate support. Demonstration can be useful, but the employee needs a chance to perform and explain the work. Otherwise the visible result does not establish learning.

items.title: All ordinary work remains unchanged
items.body: An opportunity that depends on unbounded extra labor may exclude people with less available time. Discuss the actual workload and approved options rather than praising sacrifice as the criterion. If no workable arrangement is available, reconsider scope or timing and explain the decision honestly.

tabs.label: Boundary
tabs.body: A boundary identifies the included work and decisions that belong to another role. For example, an employee may draft a comparison without authority to approve the policy it informs. Explain that difference before work begins. If the project doubles in scope, recheck the agreement and formal requirements rather than interpreting enthusiasm as unlimited availability.

tabs.label: Support
tabs.body: Support includes approved time, access, examples and a named colleague who can help without taking over. An opportunity is less usable when feedback depends on personal relationships or a contact who is never available. Agree on a fallback. The colleague’s completed product cannot be counted as the employee’s demonstrated development.

tabs.label: Review
tabs.body: Review examines the reasoning and product at a proportionate point. It should reveal whether the task and support remain workable, not wait until a large effort has failed. An expanding scope or blocked dependency may require revision through responsible roles. Hidden extra labor is not a reliable measure of ambition or a sound substitute for planning.

check.question: A project doubles in scope after an employee accepts it. What is the strongest response?
check.correct: Revisit the work boundary, workload, authority and support through the responsible process before expecting the expanded result.
wrong: Assume the employee accepted every future task by agreeing once.
Use evening work as proof of ambition.
Ask the colleague to complete everything and credit it as the employee’s development.
check.feedbackCorrect: A material change needs a workable agreement and any required authority, not an unlimited expectation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One acceptance cannot authorize every later expansion of duties. Evening work is not a fair or complete measure of ambition. A colleague completing the assignment cannot establish the employee’s development. Revisit scope, workload, authority and support through the responsible process so the employee can perform meaningful work within a workable agreement.

items.text: The colleague gives specific feedback and the employee revises the draft.
The task expands without changing time or ordinary duties.
The colleague completes every part while the employee observes without practice.
The agreement explains decisions that require review.
Participation depends on unapproved evening work.
A colleague does the analysis but it is recorded as the participant’s demonstrated skill.

lessons.next: Next, recognize the work through evidence without creating an informal promotion promise.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Priam accepts a bounded meeting-facilitation assignment. It grows into several additional reviews while his ordinary workload stays unchanged. Supervisor Nia says this is how employees prove they want advancement.
scenario.prompt: Which action makes the opportunity credible?
options: Restate scope and approved workload support, confirm authority and arrange feedback tied to Priam’s work.
Tell Priam that asking about workload shows insufficient commitment.
Give the work to a colleague but report Priam as having completed it.
responses: This makes the assignment usable and keeps the learning tied to actual performance.
A practical workload question should not become a personality judgment.
Substitution conceals the actual work and does not demonstrate Priam’s learning.

lessons.transfer: Draft an assignment agreement with result, boundary, existing-work arrangement, feedback contact, early check and changed-scope trigger. Use invented duties.

move.control: You can clarify scope, obtain authorized workload arrangements and provide feedback without taking over the employee’s work.
move.failure: The opportunity rewards hidden extra labor while learning and authority remain unclear.
move.next: Review the conditions of one current developmental assignment at the next relevant work check.

lessons.title: Recognize contribution without promising advancement
lessons.summary: Document relevant learning and contribution while keeping formal promotion decisions separate.
lessons.objective: Describe demonstrated capability using a specific work example.
objectives: Describe demonstrated capability using a specific work example.
Distinguish recognition, development feedback and formal selection evidence.
Write a next-step conversation that does not guarantee promotion.
takeaways: Credit the work that was actually done.
Future selection follows its own process.
lessons.statement: Recognition should make contribution visible without turning an assignment into a promised appointment.

image.caption: A useful review names contribution, learning and the next appropriate opportunity.

intro.heading: Make the learning and contribution visible
intro.body:
A developmental assignment can end with a thank-you message while the employee receives little usable feedback. It can also end with an exaggerated promise that the employee is now next in line for promotion. Neither response gives a clear account of what the work demonstrated. Recognition should name the contribution and the capability evidence, while keeping future employment decisions within their applicable procedures.

Review the product and the employee’s actual role. What did they do, what changed because of it and which capability became visible? If several colleagues contributed, describe the contribution fairly rather than assigning all credit to the most visible presenter. A useful account might say that the employee organized conflicting evidence, identified a missing perspective and revised a recommendation after feedback.

Ask what the employee learned and what remains uncertain. Learning is not always a smooth success; an appropriate revision or request for guidance can demonstrate judgment. Avoid recording a secret label such as “not leadership material” based on one difficulty. Formal performance documentation follows the responsible process, and these course activities should use invented examples rather than real personnel records.

Discuss future development without making guarantees. The experience may provide relevant evidence for a later application or another supported task. Explain how the employee can use that evidence and where current opportunities are found. Formal promotions and covered selections remain subject to the applicable criteria and procedures; a supervisor’s recognition does not bypass them.

Check recognition access as a process question. Are behind-the-scenes contributions made visible? Do only employees who present at high-profile meetings receive acknowledgment? Does a reader know whose work appears in a shared product? Improve the evidence trail and appropriate recognition rather than compensating through unsupported appointment promises. The goal is honest credit and useful growth.

lessons.keyStatement: Recognition names evidence; it does not guarantee an employment outcome.

items.title: The presenter receives all credit
items.body: A visible presentation may depend on others’ research, organization or follow-through. Ask who contributed what and use an accurate account. Recognition should not require everyone to adopt the same public style. Keep actual performance and personnel documentation within approved processes.

items.title: One difficulty becomes a permanent label
items.body: A developmental task includes learning. Examine the specific issue, support and revision before making a broad conclusion. Formal concerns still need their responsible process, but an informal potential label can conceal weak evidence and close future access without explanation.

items.title: Completion becomes a promotion promise
items.body: Relevant experience can support a future application, not replace the selection procedure. Explain the capability evidence and current opportunity routes. Do not imply that another candidate will be excluded or that the employee is owed an appointment because they accepted extra work.

tabs.label: Contribution
tabs.body: Contribution identifies the employee’s actual work, including preparation or reasoning less visible in a meeting. “You did well” offers encouragement but little usable evidence. Describe the relevant product and effect accurately. Public confidence should not erase a colleague’s quieter analytical contribution or become an unannounced proxy for the assignment’s purpose.

tabs.label: Learning
tabs.body: Learning concerns what the employee can now do or explain and what practice remains helpful. Invite their reasoning rather than assigning a hidden potential label. A strong product may reflect useful support as well as capability; examine their own contribution. This helps plan a next step without confusing participation with a complete assessment of the person.

tabs.label: Future
tabs.body: The future discussion explains how experience may inform an appropriate next opportunity. Recognize demonstrated capability while making the actual selection process clear. Promising advancement rewards effort with an outcome outside authority; refusing any learning discussion makes the formal boundary unnecessarily discouraging. Honest direction can support growth without offering a guarantee.

check.question: An employee completes a useful analysis and asks whether this guarantees promotion. What is the appropriate response?
check.correct: Recognize the demonstrated capability and explain that future promotion follows the applicable selection process, with this experience available as relevant evidence.
wrong: Promise promotion to reward the extra effort.
Refuse to discuss learning because formal selection is separate.
Tell the employee that only public presentation style will matter later.
check.feedbackCorrect: This provides honest recognition and useful direction while preserving formal employment procedures.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Promising promotion creates an unauthorized employment guarantee. Avoiding all learning discussion makes recognition less useful than it could be. Treating presentation style as the only future consideration substitutes a narrow proxy for relevant evidence. Recognize the demonstrated capability and explain how an appropriate next step fits the applicable process.

items.text: The employee organized the source evidence and clarified the recommendation.
Use the experience to describe relevant capability in an applicable future process.
Completing this task means the next role is yours.
The review credits the research and follow-through behind the presentation.
Check current criteria and opportunity routes with the responsible role.
Other applicants will not be considered because you did extra work.

lessons.next: Next, examine the access pattern and improve the opportunity process.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Farah prepares a strong evidence review, while colleague Peter presents it. Supervisor Ken praises Peter as the project’s sole contributor and tells Farah that her extra hours guarantee the next promotion. Neither statement matches the work or the selection rules.
options: Leave both statements because they sound positive.
Describe each contribution accurately, discuss Farah’s demonstrated capabilities and explain the actual future selection process without a guarantee.
Stop all recognition to avoid making mistakes.
responses: Positive language can still obscure contribution and make an unauthorized promise.
This provides honest credit and meaningful development guidance while preserving formal procedures.
Recognition can be useful when it is specific and accurate.

lessons.transfer: Write a closing note for a practice assignment naming actual contribution, demonstrated capability, a learning question and an appropriate next step without a guarantee.

move.control: You can give accurate credit and explain evidence-based development while respecting formal selection authority.
move.failure: Invisible work disappears and unsupported promises substitute for honest recognition.
move.next: Use a contribution-and-learning review at the end of the next developmental assignment.

lessons.title: Review the opportunity path over time
lessons.summary: Examine who can discover, use and benefit from opportunities without turning participation into a personal ranking.
lessons.objective: Select process evidence for reviewing access to developmental work.
objectives: Select process evidence for reviewing access to developmental work.
Identify a reporting limitation involving small groups or differing assignments.
Propose one improvement supported by the observed opportunity path.
takeaways: Report limits and protect employee information.
Improve a process rather than rank people.
lessons.statement: A repeated pattern should prompt a careful process review, not an assumption about ambition or culture.

image.caption: A review connects access, support and recognition with the next process improvement.

intro.heading: Look beyond who accepted the assignment
intro.body:
A supervisor may notice that the same employees receive developmental work and conclude that they are the only people who want to grow. That pattern needs examination before explanation. The same people may hear first, have lighter ordinary workloads, know the interest route or receive more encouragement. Others may choose different goals. A review should trace the opportunity path rather than attach a personal label to participation.

Choose process evidence that matches the question. Were invitations and criteria visible before choices? Could employees ask questions and express interest? Were workload and support explained? Was contribution reviewed afterward? Use approved records and minimal information. A learning dashboard should not create an informal personnel file or infer an employee’s intercultural orientation.

Compare opportunities carefully. A one-hour practice meeting is not the same commitment as a long technical project. Employees in different roles may have different eligibility or formal requirements. Seek responsible HR guidance before interpreting group differences or changing assignment procedures. A comparison is useful only when the definitions and practical context are understandable.

Protect privacy and report uncertainty. Small or distinctive roles can make employees identifiable even in an unnamed summary. Follow responsible data guidance for actual reporting rather than inventing a fixed threshold. Missing information should remain a limit, not be presented as “everyone had equal access.” Absence of an expression of interest does not tell you why the employee did not apply.

Choose one improvement supported by the evidence. It might be a clearer invitation, a workload discussion before selection, better capability criteria or a contribution review. Identify the process owner, any required authority and a check of the result at the next relevant opportunity. Consultant guidance can help staff develop this analysis, while staff carry out their own responsibilities.

lessons.keyStatement: Measure the arrangement people could use, not a hidden score of their ambition.

items.title: The same people participate
items.body: The pattern may reflect capability, interest, information or practical support; it does not identify the cause by itself. Trace each stage and ask about the process through appropriate channels. Avoid deciding that others lack ambition before examining what was available to them.

items.title: A comparison combines unlike work
items.body: Different assignments can involve different skills, commitments and procedures. State those distinctions and compare only what the evidence supports. Do not use one broad participation rate to erase meaningful differences in workload or eligibility. Responsible HR and data guidance may be needed.

items.title: A dashboard fills every gap with reassurance
items.body: Unreported or missing information does not prove fair access. Explain the limit and choose a practical process check that can be completed appropriately. Protect employee information and avoid personal cultural labels. A modest, qualified finding is more credible than a polished unsupported assurance.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: The question identifies which stage of opportunity access needs examination. Repeated assignments to two employees may lead you to ask whether others received information before selection. That is more actionable than guessing everyone else lacks ambition. Link the inquiry to an arrangement the responsible leader can examine without pre-deciding its cause.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence includes appropriate records and experience input, with definitions and privacy limits. Participation patterns may reflect information, criteria, workload or support, but the pattern alone cannot tell you which explanation applies. Missing responses remain unknown. Avoid inferring personal cultural-development labels or making private circumstances the evidence source for a broad process claim.

tabs.label: Change
tabs.body: A change addresses a supported process gap within authority, with an owner and review point. If the invitation arrived after selection, move the actual interest opportunity earlier through the applicable procedure. Check whether that makes access usable. Do not add course completion as an invented eligibility gate or promise equal career outcomes from one improvement.

check.question: Only two employees have received repeated assignments, and others did not express interest. What does this establish?
check.correct: A participation pattern that needs examination of information, criteria, workload and support; it does not establish others’ motives.
wrong: The two employees should automatically receive every future promotion.
The supervisor can assign developmental orientations to nonparticipants.
check.feedbackCorrect: The pattern supports a process inquiry with relevant evidence and limits, not a personal explanation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A participation pattern cannot establish other employees’ motives. Repeated assignment recipients are not entitled to every future promotion. Nonparticipation does not reveal an assessed intercultural orientation. Examine how information, criteria, workload and support shaped the actual opportunity, and keep interpretation within the evidence and approved information practices.

items.text: The interest route was omitted from the invitation.
The reason some employees did not apply is not known.
Nonparticipants have low ambition.
The assignment had no agreed review point.
Different role eligibility must be confirmed before comparison.
An employee’s developmental orientation is inferred from assignment attendance.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to build an explainable and usable developmental opportunity.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Anika reviews a year of developmental work. The same employees received repeated assignments, and the only record of interest was an informal conversation. Some tasks also required different technical skills. Anika wants to improve access without inventing a cause.
scenario.prompt: What is the strongest next step?
options: Name nonparticipants as unmotivated in a workforce report.
Guarantee the next assignments to employees based solely on identity.
Clarify the interest route and criteria, examine workload and support, use responsible comparison guidance and check the next opportunity’s usability.
responses: The records do not establish motivation and the label would not improve the process.
Fair access does not authorize identity-based employment decisions or bypass applicable criteria.
This addresses the process evidence and preserves responsible authority, privacy and honest limits.

lessons.transfer: Create a practice opportunity review covering discovery, criteria, selection, workload, feedback and recognition. Choose one change, owner and result check.

move.control: You can make the opportunity path clearer and obtain responsible guidance for comparisons or formal changes.
move.failure: A participation chart becomes a ranking of people while the process that produced it stays unexplained.
move.next: At the next appropriate planning cycle, review one opportunity path and implement an evidence-linked improvement.

jobAid.subtitle: A usable path from developmental purpose to fair review.
remember: Define the actual arrangement and confirm formal requirements.
Make information, criteria and support visible before choices.
Credit contribution honestly and preserve formal selection processes.

sections.heading: Define and invite
items: Name the capability, result and assignment boundary.
Confirm authority, workload and applicable employment requirements with responsible roles.
Explain the invitation, criteria, question contact and interest route before selection.
Avoid assumptions about private circumstances or communication style.

sections.heading: Choose and support
items: Compare relevant evidence against stable criteria.
Separate entry requirements from the capability being developed.
Agree on workload, access, feedback and changed-scope review.
Let the employee do and revise the work with appropriate support.

sections.heading: Recognize and review
items: Describe actual contribution and demonstrated capability.
Explain appropriate next steps without guaranteeing promotion.
Review information, choice, support and recognition through approved evidence.
Protect privacy, state limits and choose one process improvement with an owner.
